To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

a) a simplified view of streaming in algal plant cells, based on a model of myosin motors moving on fixed actin tracks, is able to account for the streaming velocity observed in experiments; and that b) the presence of a finite slip layer close to walls is important for the streaming velocity, and the presence of a wall slip layer is necessary to obtain the observed streaming velocities.
a model for cytoplasma streaming in plant cells that includes the effects of wall slip can account for the magnitude of observed streaming velocities.

a simple, purely hydrodynamic model for cytoplasmaic streaming, which does not require the presence of a motor coupling between cytoplasm and the vacuole, and does not rely on the existence of an active cytoplasmic layer, is sufficient to account for the magnitude of the streaming velocities observed experimentally in living plant cells.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the study of cytoplasmic flow in plant cells, which is driven by molecular motors.
the study of a microscopic model of cytoplasmic flow in plant cells.
the role of wall-slip in cytoplasmic microtubule streaming in plant cells.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
cytoplasmic flow in plant cells is driven by a combination of the motor activity and a wall slip layer.

, in the absence of any coupling between the cytoplasmic fluid and the actin network, a model based on the assumption of the presence of a slip layer between the endoplasm and the vacuole is sufficient to account for the experimental observations of streaming velocities in living plant cells, and that the magnitude of streaming velocity can be accounted for by a simple model in which motors are modelled as spheres undergoing Brownian motion along straight lines.

the streaming in Characeae cells is driven by the action of myosin motors moving along actin filaments, and that this action is coupled to the cytoplasmic and vacuo- lomic fluid by viscous forces, which in turn are mediated by a finite wall slip layer.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
, in the case of Chara coralla, a simple model of myosin motors moving along fixed tracks is able to explain the streaming velocities of the intracellular fluid.
the cytoplasmic flow in plant cells is driven by the motion of the myosin motors along actin tracks.

the observed magnitude of cytoplasmic flow in plant cells is a consequence of the interplay of the following physical factors: the existence of a finite slip layer in the wall of the cell; the existence of a dense network of actin filaments in the cytoplasm; the existence of myosin molecules in the cytoploplasm, which are attached to the actin filaments and which move in a directed manner along them.
The main takeaway from our work is that

, in the absence of a coupling mechanism between motors, cytosol and vacuole, it is not possible to account for the streaming velocity in the cell interior unless the boundary close to the wall is treated as a finite slip layer.
the presence of a slip layer close to a wall is crucial for explaining streaming.
the slip of the endoplasm at the wall is crucial for the generation of the large velocities of the intracellular fluid.
